title: Speed & Space
summary: How to pick a safe speed, keep a space cushion around your car, and understand how far it really takes to stop.

blocks.text: Every state has a basic speed law: never drive faster than is safe for current conditions. The posted limit is the most you may drive when conditions are ideal. It is a maximum, not a target.

Speed limits are set for normal, good conditions: dry pavement, daylight and light traffic. When it is wet, dark, foggy or crowded, you must slow down below the limit. You can get a ticket for driving too fast for conditions even if you are under the posted limit.

items: Road surface: wet, icy, gravel or bumpy roads need lower speeds.
Weather and light: rain, snow, fog, glare and darkness all mean slower.
Traffic: heavy traffic, pedestrians, bicyclists and children call for more care.
The road itself: curves, hills, narrow lanes and work zones.

blocks.text: A speed limit sign shows the maximum speed for good conditions. A NIGHT plaque below it gives a lower limit after dark. Some highways also post a minimum speed: under normal conditions, driving slower than it is illegal. If you cannot safely keep up with the minimum, use another road.

blocks.caption: Maximum and minimum speed limits on the same sign.

blocks.text: Speed limits for highways, cities, school zones and residential areas, and any minimum speeds, vary by state. Check your State Cheat Sheet for the numbers you need to know.
When light rain starts on a road that has been dry for a while, oil on the pavement makes it very slick. Slow down and add following distance.
Crashes are more likely when vehicles travel at very different speeds. The safest choice is usually to move with the flow of traffic while staying within the speed limit.

items: Driving much slower than everyone else is also dangerous. Drivers behind you may brake suddenly or make risky passes.
If traffic is moving faster than the limit, do not speed up to match it. Stay at or below the limit and keep to the right.
On a road with two or more lanes in your direction, use the right lane if you drive slower than other traffic.
On a two-lane road, if a line of cars builds up behind you, pull over where it is safe, such as a turnout, and let them pass.
When someone is passing you, keep right and do not speed up. Let them finish the pass.

sections.heading: Your space cushion and following distance

blocks.text: A space cushion is open space on all sides of your car: ahead, behind and to each side. It gives you time to see problems and room to react. The space ahead is the part you control the most, because you choose how closely you follow.
Following too closely is the most common cause of rear-end crashes. Use the counting method to check your gap:

items: Pick a fixed object ahead, such as a road sign or utility pole.
When the rear of the vehicle ahead passes it, start counting: one-thousand-one, one-thousand-two, and so on.
Stop counting when the front of your car reaches the same object.
If you reach the object before you finish your state's recommended count, you are too close. Ease off the gas, drop back and count again.

blocks.text: Counting seconds works better than trying to keep a set number of feet. At higher speeds you cover more ground each second, so a time gap grows in feet automatically as you go faster.
The number of seconds handbooks recommend varies by state. Check your State Cheat Sheet, and treat it as a minimum for good conditions.

rows: Wet, icy or snowy roads
Tires have less grip, so you need more distance to stop.
Night, fog or heavy rain
You see hazards later, so give yourself more time.
Behind a large truck
It blocks your view. Drop back so you can see around it.
Behind a school bus or hazmat truck
They may have to stop at railroad crossings.
Behind a motorcycle
It can stop very quickly, and the rider could fall on a rough surface.
Pulling a trailer or heavy load
Extra weight means it takes longer to stop.
Going down a long, steep hill
Gravity works against your brakes.
Stopped on a steep uphill
The car ahead may roll back when it starts.
Work zones
Traffic often slows or stops suddenly.
Being tailgated
More room ahead lets you slow gradually.

sections.heading: How far it takes to stop

blocks.text: Total stopping distance has three parts:

rows: Perception distance
How far you travel from the moment your eyes see a hazard until your brain recognizes it.
Reaction distance
How far you travel from seeing the hazard until your foot presses the brake.
Braking distance
How far you travel from the moment the brakes are applied until the car stops.

blocks.text: Speed makes a big difference. If you double your speed, for example from 30 mph to 60 mph, your reaction distance doubles, but your braking distance becomes about four times as long. The force of impact in a crash also becomes about four times as great.

items: Reaction distance grows when you are tired, distracted or impaired.
Braking distance depends on speed, the condition of your tires and brakes, and the road surface. A wet road makes it longer.
To cut your reaction time when you see trouble ahead, such as brake lights or a child near the road, take your foot off the gas and hold it over the brake pedal.

blocks.text: Overdriving your headlights means driving so fast that you cannot stop within the distance your headlights light up. At night, slow down until you can. In fog or any low visibility, drive slowly enough to stop within the distance you can see.
Higher speeds also narrow your field of vision, so you notice less at the sides of the road.

items: On a road with more than one lane your way, move right when it is safe and let the tailgater pass.
On a two-lane road where you cannot change lanes, increase the space ahead of you. Then slow down gently when the road is clear so the driver can pass.
Extra space ahead lets you slow gradually instead of stopping suddenly, which could get you hit from behind.
Help drivers behind you keep a safe gap: hold a steady speed and signal early before you slow down or turn.
If a car cuts into the space in front of you, ease off the accelerator to rebuild a safe gap. Do not brake hard.

blocks.text: Never brake suddenly to 'teach' a tailgater a lesson. It can cause the very crash you are trying to avoid.

Slow down before you enter a curve, while your car is still going straight. Braking in the middle of a curve can make the car skid. Curves are where too much speed on a slippery road most often causes drivers to lose control.

items: An advisory speed on a curve sign is for good conditions. On a wet or icy road, go slower than the advisory speed.
Enter the curve slowly enough that you can keep a light, steady pressure on the gas as you go through it. Speed up gently only after the middle of the curve.
If you realize partway through a curve that you are going too fast, ease off the gas, brake gently only if needed, and keep steering through the curve.
When you near the top of a hill and cannot see beyond it, slow down and be ready to stop. A stalled car or other hazard could be just over the crest.

blocks.text: An escape route is open space you could steer into to avoid a hazard. Good drivers always know where theirs is.

items: On a multi-lane road, do not drive right alongside another vehicle for long. You may be in its blind spot, and neither of you has room to move.
If you are boxed in by a pack of vehicles, ease off slightly and let the pack move ahead of you.
When there is no open space on either side of your car, increase your following distance ahead.
Pass a row of parked cars with as much room as you safely can. A door may open, or a person or car may pull out.

blocks.text: Handle one hazard at a time. If a bicyclist is ahead on your right and an oncoming car is coming, slow down, let the car pass, then move over to give the bicyclist room.

keyPoints: Never drive faster than is safe for conditions; posted limits assume ideal conditions.
Keep pace with traffic within the limit, and use the right lane if you are slower.
Check following distance by counting seconds past a fixed object; your state's recommended seconds are on your State Cheat Sheet.
Leave extra space in bad weather, at night, behind trucks, motorcycles and school buses, and when towing.
Doubling your speed doubles reaction distance but makes braking distance and impact force about four times greater.
Do not overdrive your headlights: always be able to stop within the distance you can see.
Slow down before a curve, not in it, and slow down near hilltops you cannot see over.
Let tailgaters pass, and always keep an escape route open around your car.
